messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John is a 67-year-old North American man who has been working as a hotel manager for over three decades. His long-standing career and marital stability have provided him with a sense of routine and security—until he was mugged in his hotel parking garage one evening last year. The traumatic event left John feeling permanently altered, particularly because the mugger had threatened him repeatedly during the attack while other patrons of the hotel stood by and did not intervene. Since the incident, John has become hypervigilant. He describes himself as being superalert or watchful all the time, even when he is inside his own home. This hyperarousal has made it difficult for him to relax in any environment. He now starts at loud noises and reacts with alarm if someone touches him unexpectedly. These heightened responses are often triggered by perceived threats such as people acting suspiciously, which have become increasingly common in John’s mind. The traumatic experience has also left John with deep feelings of mistrust towards others and a belief that the world is a dangerous place. He feels permanently humiliated by what happened, believing he was helpless and vulnerable. These negative appraisals exacerbate his sense of threat; he constantly feels as though danger could arise at any moment. This constant state of alertness has led to significant avoidance behaviors. John avoids going out alone and often stays late at work to avoid the parking garage during evening hours when it is more likely to be deserted. John’s negative appraisals have significantly contributed to his sense of threat, leading him to overestimate risks in everyday situations. For instance, he finds himself constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of potential threats even while managing hotel operations. His colleagues notice that he appears tense and distracted during meetings, often checking the door or looking at windows as if expecting someone to enter with hostile intentions. The smell of alcohol is another potent trigger for John; it reminds him of the night when the mugger had been drinking heavily and became aggressive. Now, whenever he encounters this scent, even in social settings at work, he becomes anxious and irritable. He avoids attending hotel events where alcohol is served, which has strained his professional relationships with staff members who have come to see his absence as a sign of disinterest or aloofness. John’s hypervigilance and heightened startle response have also affected his home life. His wife notes that he reacts sharply when she approaches him from behind without warning and becomes irritable if there are loud noises in the neighborhood, such as fireworks on holidays. This has made their shared space feel less safe and more tense. Despite these difficulties, John’s decision to seek help came after a particularly distressing incident at work where a group of rowdy guests had been drinking heavily and acting aggressively. He felt overwhelmed by memories of his mugging and became extremely anxious, nearly losing control in front of staff and guests. This episode made him realize that he needed professional support to manage his symptoms. John’s current state is one of profound fear and uncertainty about the future. While he acknowledges the need for help, he is most afraid of being vulnerable again and not knowing how to protect himself from potential threats. He hopes therapy will provide tools to manage his hypervigilance and negative beliefs so that he can regain a sense of security in both his professional and personal life.
